q: Which term describes monocular technique for eccentric fixation; uses intense light to dazzle peripheral retina and rehabilitate foveal fixation?
w: Pleoptics: Greek pleion (more) + ops. Monocular technique for eccentric fixation; uses intense light to dazzle peripheral retina and rehabilitate foveal fixation
k: Pleoptics = Monocular technique for eccentric fixation; uses intense light to dazzle peripheral retina and reh

q: Which term describes fixation in the amblyopic eye at a retinal point other than the fovea; marker of deep amblyopia?
w: Eccentric fixation: Latin ex-centrum (off-center). Fixation in the amblyopic eye at a retinal point other than the fovea; marker of deep amblyopia
k: Eccentric fixation = Fixation in the amblyopic eye at a retinal point other than the fovea; marker of deep amb

q: Which term describes normal doubling of non-fixated objects; expected finding when fusion is intact; absent when suppression is present?
w: Physiological diplopia: Greek diploos (double). Normal doubling of non-fixated objects; expected finding when fusion is intact; absent when suppression is present
k: Physiological diplopia = Normal doubling of non-fixated objects; expected finding when fusion is intact; absen

q: Which term describes step 3 of Parks test; tilting the head increases vertical fusion demand on cyclovertical muscles of the ipsilateral eye?
w: Bielschowsky head tilt test: Named: Alfred Bielschowsky (1900s). Step 3 of Parks test; tilting the head increases vertical fusion demand on cyclovertical muscles of the ipsilateral eye
k: Bielschowsky head tilt test = Step 3 of Parks test; tilting the head increases vertical fusion demand on cyclo

q: Which term describes instrument for measuring objective and subjective angle of deviation and training at all three Grades of BV?
w: Synoptophore / Amblyoscope: Greek synoptos (seen together). Instrument for measuring objective and subjective angle of deviation and training at all three Grades of BV
k: Synoptophore / Amblyoscope = Instrument for measuring objective and subjective angle of deviation and training

q: Which term describes rotating high-contrast gratings; spatially stimulates amblyopic eye monocularly; 7 min/session?
w: CAM vision stimulator: Cambridge (Univ.) Amblyopia Model. Rotating high-contrast gratings; spatially stimulates amblyopic eye monocularly; 7 min/session
k: CAM vision stimulator = Rotating high-contrast gratings; spatially stimulates amblyopic eye monocularly; 7 min

q: Which term describes presents different images to each eye simultaneously; forces cortical integration; modern active amblyopia therapy?
w: Dichoptic training: Greek dikha (separately) + optikos. Presents different images to each eye simultaneously; forces cortical integration; modern active amblyopia therapy
k: Dichoptic training = Presents different images to each eye simultaneously; forces cortical integration; modern

q: In OEP analysis, which refractive condition BUFFERS the accommodative pattern?
w: OEP pairs each pattern with the error that cushions it: hyperopia buffers the accommodative pattern, exophoria buffers the convergence pattern. Recognising the buffer tells you which pattern the case is really about.
k: Hyperopia buffers accommodation; exophoria buffers convergence.

q: In OEP analysis, which condition BUFFERS the convergence pattern?
w: Exophoria buffers convergence, hyperopia buffers accommodation. The convergence pattern is the mechanism for maintaining single vision, so the phoria that relieves convergence demand is the buffer.
k: Exophoria buffers the convergence pattern.

q: On OEP probe testing, a CONVEX lens inhibits accommodation and makes the target appear:
w: Plus inhibits accommodation: the object seems to move AWAY and appears BIGGER. Minus stimulates accommodation: the object seems to come CLOSER and appears SMALLER. Base-in behaves like plus, base-out like minus.
k: Plus/BI: away + bigger. Minus/BO: closer + smaller.

q: On OEP probe testing, BASE-OUT prism stimulates convergence and makes the target appear:
w: Base-out stimulates convergence, so the object seems to approach and shrink, mirroring a minus lens. Base-in inhibits convergence and mirrors a plus lens: away and bigger.
k: BO = closer + smaller (like minus); BI = away + bigger (like plus).

q: OEP test #3 is performed at 20 feet with which lenses in place?
w: #3 uses the habitual correction and measures lateral imbalance at far as the patient currently lives it. #8 repeats the measurement at far but through the test #7 lenses, so the pair shows what the new prescription changed.
k: #3 = habitual Rx; #8 = through the #7 Rx.

q: What is the primary purpose of case history in optometric practice?
o: To gather information about the patient's ocular and systemic condition
To measure the patient's pupillary distance for lens fitting
To determine the best spectacle frame size and shape for them
To determine the thickness of the finished spectacle lenses
w: History collects symptoms, ocular and systemic background to guide the exam and diagnosis. Frame size, PD and lens thickness are dispensing measurements, not the purpose of history.
k: "Case history" = talking and gathering information. Pick the option about collecting patient information, not a physical measurement.

q: Which is considered a subjective test of visual acuity?
w: Snellen relies on the patient's responses, so it is subjective. Retinoscopy, autorefraction and keratometry are objective, machine or examiner readings that need no patient judgement of clarity.
k: "Subjective" = depends on the patient reporting. The chart the patient reads (Snellen) is subjective; instruments that measure without patient opinion are objective.

q: The standard Snellen distance visual acuity is commonly measured at:
w: Standard testing distance is 6 m (about 20 feet), taken as optical infinity for the eye. 1 and 3 m are near/intermediate; 12 m is nonstandard.
k: 20 feet equals 6 meters, the classic distance-acuity setup. That is the number to reach for.

q: Which test measures the ability to see fine detail?
w: Visual acuity quantifies resolution of fine detail. Tonometry is pressure, keratometry is corneal curvature, cover test is alignment.
k: "Fine detail" is the definition of acuity. Match the phrase to the test with the same meaning.

q: Which instrument is used for objective measurement of refractive error?
w: Retinoscopy objectively estimates refractive error from the reflex, without patient responses. Tonometer measures IOP, ophthalmoscope views the fundus, trial frame holds lenses for subjective testing.
k: "Objective" plus "refractive error" points to retinoscopy. The trial frame is for the subjective step, not objective measurement.

q: During retinoscopy, a "with motion" reflex generally indicates:
o: The eye has no refractive error
The far point is behind the retinoscope
w: With movement means the far point lies behind the examiner, needing plus to neutralise (hyperopic side of neutrality). High myopia gives against movement; emmetropia gives neutral at the far point; opacity dulls the reflex.
k: With = far point behind you (add plus); against = far point in front (add minus). Translate the reflex direction into far-point location.

q: Which test is used to detect binocular alignment problems?
w: The cover test reveals phorias and tropias (misalignment). Ishihara is colour, Schirmer is tears, Amsler is central/macular field.
k: "Alignment" = how the two eyes point together = cover test. The others test colour, tears, or macula.

q: The Maddox rod is primarily used to assess:
w: The Maddox rod dissociates the eyes to measure phoria. It has nothing to do with colour, pressure or curvature.
k: Maddox rod produces a line to compare against a light, a phoria/alignment tool. Alignment wording is the match.

q: Which test is commonly used to assess stereopsis?
w: The Titmus (fly/circles) test grades stereopsis (depth). Amsler is macular field, Ishihara is colour, Schirmer is tears.
k: Stereopsis = depth from two eyes. Titmus is the classic depth-perception test; the rest test other functions.

q: The Ishihara test is primarily used to assess:
w: Ishihara plates screen red-green colour vision. Acuity is Snellen, binocular status is cover/Worth, accommodation is amplitude testing.
k: Ishihara = coloured dot plates = colour vision. Straight tool-to-function match.

q: Which test is commonly used to assess central visual function?
w: The Amsler grid checks the central 10 degrees for scotomas and metamorphopsia (macular function). Cover test is alignment, Worth 4-dot is fusion, Schirmer is tears.
k: "Central visual function" = macula = Amsler grid. Distortion or central blur points here.

q: The Worth 4-dot test is used mainly to evaluate:
w: Worth 4-dot assesses fusion and suppression using red/green dissociation. It is unrelated to curvature, tears or pressure.
k: Four dots seen through red-green glasses test whether the eyes fuse. "Fusion/binocular" is the keyword.

q: Which instrument is used to measure intraocular pressure?
w: Tonometry measures IOP. Retinoscope estimates refraction, lensometer reads spectacle power, keratometer reads corneal curvature.
k: Prefix "tono-" refers to pressure/tension, so tonometer = pressure meter.

q: A normal intraocular pressure is approximately:
w: Normal IOP is 10 to 21 mmHg. Below 10 trends to hypotony; 25 to 40 is glaucoma-range.
k: Same 10 to 21 band as the anatomy set. Anchor it and reject values far outside.

q: Which instrument provides a magnified, illuminated view of the eye?
w: The slit lamp gives a magnified, illuminated, sectioned view of ocular structures. Lensometer reads lenses, retinoscope estimates refraction, trial frame holds lenses.
k: "Magnified + illuminated view of the eye" is the slit lamp's definition. The others do not image the eye.

q: Fluorescein staining is particularly useful for detecting:
w: Fluorescein pools in and highlights epithelial breaks (abrasions, ulcers, dry-eye staining). Cataract, detachment and presbyopia are not surface-dye findings.
k: A surface dye shows surface damage. Match fluorescein to the epithelial/corneal option.

q: Which test evaluates tear production?
w: The Schirmer strip measures aqueous tear production. Amsler is macula, Maddox rod is phoria, Ishihara is colour.
k: Schirmer = paper strip wetting = tears. Any "tear/dry eye" stem points here.

q: The first step before performing most clinical tests is to:
o: Immediately perform tonometry to measure the eye pressure
Dilate the pupil right away using mydriatic eyedrops
Prescribe corrective lenses before any testing is done
Explain the procedure and obtain appropriate patient cooperation
w: Explaining the test and gaining cooperation (and consent) comes first for reliable, ethical testing. Dilation, prescribing and tonometry are specific later steps, not the universal first move.
k: "First step, most tests" wants the general prerequisite: communicate and get cooperation. Specific procedures are too narrow to be the first step for everything.

q: In subjective refraction, which technique is commonly used to determine the patient's best spherical correction?
w: Fogging relaxes accommodation, then power is refined to best sphere. Schirmer, fluorescein and gonioscopy assess tears, epithelium and the angle, not sphere.
k: The stem is about refining sphere, a refraction technique. Only fogging/refinement is a refraction step; the rest are diagnostic tests.

q: The Jackson Cross Cylinder (JCC) is primarily used to refine:
w: The JCC fine-tunes astigmatic axis and power during subjective refraction. It has no role in pupil size, IOP or tears.
k: "Cross cylinder" tells you it deals with cylinder, so axis and power of astigmatism is the answer.

q: During subjective refraction, the patient should generally be encouraged to:
w: Refraction relies on the patient comparing two views and reporting which is clearer (which is better, 1 or 2). Guessing blindly, closing eyes or looking away defeats the test.
k: Subjective testing needs comparison feedback. Pick the option where the patient compares and reports.

q: What is the purpose of fogging during refraction?
w: Fogging adds plus to blur distance vision, relaxing accommodation so latent hyperopia is not masked. It does the opposite of inducing accommodation and is unrelated to IOP or curvature.
k: Extra plus blurs and relaxes focusing. "Fog" the eye to switch accommodation off, not on.

q: A pinhole test is useful because it can:
o: Improve visual acuity reduced by refractive error
Determine the patient's tear production rate
Measure the amplitude of accommodation directly
w: A pinhole blocks peripheral blurred rays, so acuity improves if the cause is refractive. It measures neither pressure, tears nor accommodation.
k: Pinhole narrows the beam and sharpens focus. Its value is separating refractive blur from other causes.

q: If visual acuity improves significantly with pinhole, the likely cause is:
w: Improvement with pinhole means blur was optical, that is uncorrected refractive error. Retinal, optic nerve or perforation causes would not improve, and may worsen, with a pinhole.
k: Pinhole better = fixable with lenses = refractive error. Pinhole no better = suspect pathology.

q: What is the primary purpose of binocular balancing?
o: Measure the central corneal thickness precisely
Determine the diameter of the patient's pupil
Measure the intraocular pressure within each eye
Equalize accommodation between the eyes during refraction
w: Balancing equalises accommodative effort between the two eyes so neither is over- or under-plussed. It is a refraction step, unrelated to IOP, pachymetry or pupil size.
k: "Binocular balancing" = making the two eyes' focus equal. The word "balance" between eyes is the clue.

q: A lensometer is used to determine:
w: A lensometer reads spectacle lens power, cylinder axis and prism. Curvature is keratometry, tears are Schirmer, retinal sensitivity is perimetry.
k: "Lens-o-meter" measures a lens (the spectacle), giving its power, axis and prism.

q: Pupillary distance is important primarily for:
w: PD aligns the optical centres of lenses with the pupils to avoid unwanted prism. It is a fitting measurement, not a diagnostic one.
k: PD is a dispensing number, so its purpose is lens fitting (centration), not disease detection.

q: A patient reports blurred distance vision that improves when squinting. Which condition is most likely?
w: Squinting creates a pinhole effect that sharpens distance blur, classic for myopia. Hyperopes and presbyopes struggle more at near; emmetropes have no blur to improve.
k: Blurred distance + squint helps (pinhole) = myopia. Squinting mimics a pinhole, and pinhole helps refractive blur.

q: A 45-year-old patient has difficulty reading small print at near but has good distance vision. The most likely diagnosis is:
w: Age around 40 to 45 with failing near vision and intact distance is presbyopia (loss of accommodation). Myopia blurs distance; keratoconus distorts vision; amblyopia is developmental reduced acuity.
k: Near trouble + age in the 40s + good distance is the presbyopia signature. Let the age drive the answer.

q: A patient complains that straight lines appear distorted or blurred differently in different orientations. This is suggestive of:
w: Orientation-dependent blur/distortion reflects unequal power in different meridians, that is astigmatism. Presbyopia is near-only; emmetropia has no error; colour deficiency affects hue, not line orientation.
k: "Different in different orientations/meridians" is the astigmatism tell. Meridian-dependent blur means cylinder.

q: A central scotoma is a defect located in the:
w: A central scotoma is a blind or dim patch in the middle of the visual field, where central vision lives. It is not in the far periphery, and it has nothing to do with the eyelids.
k: 'Central' in the name fixes the location. Pick the central field option and ignore periphery or lid distractors.

q: The Jackson cross-cylinder is primarily used to refine:
w: The Jackson cross-cylinder flips a small cylinder to compare two orientations, so it refines cylinder axis and power in subjective refraction. It has nothing to do with pupil size, fields, or color.
k: JCC equals cylinder axis and power fine-tuning. If the stem names the cross-cylinder, the answer is about astigmatism.

q: The fogging technique is used to:
w: Fogging adds plus power to blur distance vision, which relaxes accommodation so the refraction is not falsely minus. Stimulating accommodation would do the opposite, and it does not measure pressure or color.
k: Fog with plus to relax focusing. The purpose is always to switch accommodation off, not on.

q: Which filter enhances the visibility of fluorescein?
w: Fluorescein glows brightest under cobalt-blue light, so that filter is used to see corneal staining and lens fits. Red, green, and neutral-density filters do not excite the dye.
k: Fluorescein plus cobalt blue go together. When the question pairs the dye with a filter, pick cobalt blue.

q: A yellow barrier filter is used with fluorescein to:
w: A yellow barrier filter blocks the blue excitation light and passes the green-yellow glow, so fluorescein stands out with more contrast. It does not measure curvature, lens power, or pressure.
k: Yellow barrier equals more fluorescein contrast. It is an enhancer, not a measuring device.

q: RAPD is also commonly called:
w: A relative afferent pupillary defect is the Marcus Gunn pupil, seen on the swinging-flashlight test when one optic nerve is weaker. Argyll Robertson, Adie, and tonic pupils are different pupil syndromes.
k: RAPD equals Marcus Gunn. The swinging-light defect has that eponym; the other names are unrelated pupils.

q: Which chart is specifically designed for children who cannot read letters?
w: The Tumbling E chart shows the letter E in different rotations, so illiterate patients or children just point which way it opens. ETDRS uses letters, Ishihara tests color, and Amsler tests the macula.
k: Cannot read letters equals Tumbling E (or Landolt C). Pick the direction-pointing chart.

q: The Tumbling E chart requires the patient to identify the:
w: On the Tumbling E chart the patient reports which way the E points, up, down, left, or right. Color, size, and counting are not what it tests.
k: Tumbling E equals report the direction. The task is orientation, not reading or color.

q: A pachymeter is especially useful for measuring:
w: A pachymeter measures corneal thickness, important before refractive surgery and in glaucoma. It does not measure lens diameter, lens power, or pupil size.
k: 'Pachy' means thick, so corneal thickness. The root gives the answer.

q: Fluorescein is commonly used to detect:
w: Fluorescein pools in breaks of the corneal epithelium and glows, revealing abrasions and ulcers. It does not measure refractive error, color vision, or detect detachment.
k: Fluorescein equals surface (epithelial) defects. Any deep-eye or refractive option is wrong.

q: Which refractive error is corrected primarily with a minus spherical lens?
w: Myopia focuses light in front of the retina, so a diverging minus spherical lens pushes the focus back. Hyperopia needs plus, presbyopia needs reading adds, and aphakia needs strong plus.
k: Minus lens equals myopia correction. Match the diverging lens to the eye that focuses too soon.

q: A yellow barrier filter used with fluorescein primarily:
w: The yellow barrier filter boosts how clearly fluorescein shows up by cutting the blue reflection. It does not measure curvature or pressure.
k: Yellow barrier equals enhance fluorescein visibility. It is an enhancer, never a measuring tool.

q: The patient's history of present visual complaints is obtained through:
w: The patient's account of the present visual complaint is gathered by taking a case history. Tonometry, keratometry, and cover test are objective measurements, not the history.
k: Patient's story equals case history. The instrument tests measure, they do not collect the complaint.

q: Which condition occurs when the eye has unequal refractive power in different meridians?
w: When the two principal meridians of the eye have different focusing power, the result is astigmatism. Myopia and hyperopia are uniform errors, and presbyopia is an age-related focusing loss.
k: Unequal power in different meridians equals astigmatism. Uniform-error names (myopia/hyperopia) do not fit 'different meridians'.

q: A fluorescein strip is used primarily to:
o: Estimate the spherical equivalent refractive error
Determine the back vertex power of a lens
Evaluate tear film and lens-cornea interaction
Measure central corneal thickness in microns
w: A fluorescein strip stains the tear film so you can judge tear breakup and how a lens sits against the cornea. It does not measure refractive error, thickness, or lens power.
k: Fluorescein strip equals tear film and lens-cornea assessment. It stains, it does not measure numbers.

q: The Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test evaluates:
w: The Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test has patients arrange colored caps in order, grading fine color discrimination. It does not test fields, depth, or convergence.
k: '100 Hue' means color sorting. Any test named for hue or color caps is color discrimination, not a field or depth test.

q: Confrontation testing is a basic method of assessing:
w: Confrontation is a quick screen where the examiner compares the patient's field to their own, checking the visual field. It is not a color, accommodation, or curvature test.
k: Confrontation equals gross visual field screen. Face-to-face wiggling-finger testing checks fields.

q: A perimeter is an instrument used to measure:
w: A perimeter maps the visual field by finding where the patient can and cannot see targets. It does not measure acuity, corneal thickness, or lens power.
k: Perimeter equals visual field mapper. The root 'perimeter' means the edges of vision.

q: Perimetry can detect defects involving the:
w: Perimetry samples the whole field, so it detects peripheral field loss from glaucoma or neuro disease. It is not a lid, lens, or tear-film test.
k: Perimetry equals field, including the periphery. Match it to field defects, not surface structures.

q: The magnification system of a slit lamp allows the examiner to:
o: Alter the eye's refractive error during viewing
Change the curvature of the corneal surface
View ocular structures in greater detail
w: Higher magnification on the slit lamp lets the examiner see fine ocular detail. It does not raise pressure, reshape the cornea, or change refraction.
k: Magnification equals see more detail. It is an imaging aid, not something that alters the eye.

q: Which ocular structure can be examined with a slit lamp?
o: Only the extraocular muscles and orbit
Only the peripheral retina and optic disc
The cornea, anterior chamber, and lens
Only the lacrimal gland and drainage system
w: The slit lamp examines the cornea, anterior chamber, and lens together, covering the whole anterior segment. The retina and optic disc need an ophthalmoscope, and the muscles, orbit, and lacrimal system are outside its view.
k: Slit lamp equals the anterior segment as a whole: cornea, chamber, and lens. Choose the option naming the front structures together, not a single deep part.

q: The slit lamp is also called a:
w: The slit lamp is a biomicroscope, combining a microscope with a slit beam. A keratometer measures curvature, a retinoscope finds refraction, and a focimeter reads lens power.
k: Slit lamp equals biomicroscope. The 'bio-microscope' name matches its microscope-plus-light design.

q: The pinhole test is primarily used to determine whether reduced visual acuity is:
o: Due to refractive error or optical factors
Due to an inherited color-vision deficiency
Due to advanced open-angle glaucoma damage
Due to a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
w: If a pinhole sharpens vision, the blur was optical (refractive), because the pinhole cuts out blur circles. Color loss, detachment, and glaucoma would not improve with a pinhole.
k: Pinhole improves equals refractive cause. If a tiny hole helps, the problem is focus, not disease.

q: The duochrome test is based primarily on:
w: The duochrome test relies on chromatic aberration: the eye focuses red slightly behind and green slightly in front of the retina, so the two backgrounds balance the endpoint. Spherical aberration, diffraction, and polarization are not the basis.
k: Duochrome equals chromatic aberration (red vs green focus). The color split is the working principle.

q: In the duochrome test, the patient is usually shown:
w: The duochrome test shows letters on red and green backgrounds and asks which is clearer, balancing the sphere. Blue/yellow, black/white, and red/blue are not used.
k: Duochrome equals red and green backgrounds. Remember RAM-GAP: on red add minus, on green add plus.

q: The near point of convergence (NPC) measures the closest point at which:
o: The eyes can no longer accommodate on the target
The patient can maintain binocular single vision
The pupil constricts to a near light stimulus
The retina first responds to a bright stimulus
w: Near point of convergence is the closest point the eyes can turn in and still keep single vision before one drifts out. It is about fusion, not accommodation, pupils, or retina.
k: NPC equals closest point of single binocular vision. It tests convergence to break, not focusing.

q: The chief complaint refers to:
o: The patient's main reason for seeking care
w: The chief complaint is the patient's own main reason for the visit, in their words. It is not the examiner's diagnosis, the pressure, or the refraction.
k: Chief complaint equals the patient's main problem. It is subjective and patient-stated, not a measurement.

q: Which preliminary test is particularly useful for assessing the central visual field and macula?
w: The Amsler grid probes the central 10 degrees and the macula, catching central distortion. Ishihara is color, Maddox rod is alignment, Schirmer is tears.
k: Central field and macula equals Amsler grid. Central-vision questions point to the grid.

q: Which sequence best represents a typical preliminary eye examination?
o: Case history, visual acuity, pupils, binocular/other screening tests, then ocular health screening
Contact lens fitting and dispensing first, then surgery, and finally visual acuity
Diagnostic surgery, then visual acuity measurement, followed by a brief case history
Tonometry and minor surgery first, with the patient's case history taken at the very end
w: A logical prelim exam runs history first, then acuity, pupils, other binocular/screening tests, and health screening, moving from least to most invasive. Sequences that start with surgery or contact fitting are nonsense.
k: History always comes first, invasive steps last. Reject any order that opens with surgery or fitting.

q: The Worth 4 Dot test is primarily used to assess:
w: The Worth 4 Dot checks whether both eyes fuse or one suppresses, a test of binocular sensory fusion. It is not a curvature, acuity, or pressure test.
k: Worth 4 Dot equals fusion and suppression. Dots seen through red/green goggles test sensory binocularity.

q: The Worth 4 Dot test uses how many lights?
w: The Worth 4 Dot uses four lights: two green, one red, one white. Not two, three, or six.
k: The name says four. Count is fixed at four dots.

q: The stereopsis test measures:
w: A stereopsis test measures depth perception from the slight disparity between the two eyes' images. It is not color, contrast, or plain acuity.
k: Stereopsis equals depth perception. The 'stereo' root means three-dimensional seeing.

q: The Ishihara test is primarily used to detect:
w: Ishihara plates screen for red-green color deficiency, the common inherited type. They do not detect glaucoma, macular disease, or binocular problems.
k: Ishihara equals red-green color screen. Hidden-number color plates test color vision.

q: Ishihara plates are examples of:
w: Ishihara plates are pseudoisochromatic: dots of confusing colors hide a figure that color-deficient eyes miss. They are not acuity, stereo, or contrast charts.
k: Ishihara equals pseudoisochromatic plates. The technical name describes the same color-dot design.

q: A patient with red-green color deficiency may have difficulty identifying:
o: The base-apex direction of an ophthalmic prism
The exact location of the physiological blind spot
Certain numbers or patterns on Ishihara plates
Large high-contrast letters on a Snellen chart
w: Red-green deficiency makes the hidden numbers or trails on Ishihara plates hard to read. It does not blur Snellen letters, prism direction, or the blind spot.
k: Color deficiency shows up on color plates, not on black-letter charts. Match the difficulty to Ishihara.

q: The principal use of a slit lamp biomicroscope is to:
w: The slit lamp biomicroscope is built to examine the anterior segment in detail. It does not read spectacle power, blood pressure, or axial length.
k: Slit lamp equals anterior segment exam. Its core job is looking at the front of the eye.

q: The Schirmer test is primarily used to evaluate:
w: The Schirmer test measures tear production by how far a paper strip wets in the lower lid. It is not an acuity, color, or binocular test.
k: Schirmer equals tear volume. Paper strip in the lid means aqueous tear production.

q: A fluorescein test can be used to evaluate:
w: Fluorescein stains epithelial breaks and outlines the tear film, so it evaluates corneal staining and tears. It is not a field, color, or accommodation test.
k: Fluorescein equals corneal staining and tear film. The dye highlights surface and tears.

q: The tear breakup time (TBUT) evaluates:
w: Tear breakup time measures how long the tear film stays intact before dry spots appear, so it grades tear film stability. It is not acuity, retina, or color.
k: TBUT equals tear film stability (quality). It times how fast the film breaks up, not how much tear there is.

q: The red reflex test is useful for detecting abnormalities involving the:
w: An abnormal or absent red reflex points to something blocking the ocular media, such as cataract or corneal opacity. Lids, muscles, and lacrimal gland are not what it screens.
k: Red reflex equals clarity of the media. A dull reflex means an opacity in the light path.

q: The swinging flashlight test is used to assess:
w: The swinging flashlight test moves light between eyes to compare pupil responses, checking the afferent light pathway. It is not a color, curvature, or accommodation test.
k: Swinging flashlight equals pupil light response (RAPD). It compares the two afferent limbs.

q: An afferent pupillary defect is also called a:
w: An afferent pupillary defect is the relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), a weaker constriction on the affected side. It is not an accommodative, corneal, or binocular defect.
k: Afferent pupil defect equals RAPD. The input-side pupil problem is the relative afferent one.

q: The non-contact tonometer measures IOP using:
w: A non-contact tonometer flattens the cornea with a puff of air to estimate pressure without touching the eye. It does not use ultrasound, dye, or infrared to measure IOP.
k: Non-contact tonometer equals air puff. No touch means the air-puff method.

q: Which test evaluates the pupil's response to light?
o: The Amsler central field grid test
w: The pupillary light reflex test shines light to watch the pupil constrict, assessing that reflex. Ishihara, Amsler, and duochrome test color or vision, not the pupil.
k: Pupil response to light equals the light reflex test. Match the pupil to its own reflex test.

q: When light is directed into one eye, constriction of the same pupil is called the:
w: Constriction of the same eye that is lit is the direct response. The opposite eye's constriction is consensual, and near or vestibular responses are different reflexes.
k: Same eye lit and constricting equals direct. Same side = direct, other side = consensual.

q: Constriction of the opposite pupil when light is directed into one eye is called the:
w: When one eye is lit and the other pupil also constricts, that is the consensual response, from crossed pathway fibers. It is not the direct, accommodation, or blink response.
k: Opposite pupil constricting equals consensual. The unlit eye reacting is the consensual limb.

q: The swinging flashlight test is particularly useful for detecting:
o: Axial myopia in a young adult patient
w: The swinging flashlight test best reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect by showing a pupil that dilates as light swings to it. Myopia, astigmatism, and presbyopia are refractive, not pupil, findings.
k: Swinging flashlight equals detect RAPD. Refractive errors have nothing to do with this test.

q: Which instrument can be used to measure the dimensions of the palpebral aperture?
w: The palpebral aperture (lid opening) is measured with a simple ruler or gauge in millimeters. A lensometer, radiuscope, or pachymeter measures other things.
k: Lid opening equals ruler measurement. A linear distance needs a ruler, not an optical instrument.

q: Which test is commonly used to measure distance visual acuity?
w: Distance visual acuity is measured with a Snellen chart of graded letters at 6 m. Ishihara is color, Amsler is macula, Maddox rod is alignment.
k: Distance acuity equals Snellen chart. The letter chart at 6 m is the standard acuity test.

q: Visual acuity of 6/6 means the patient:
o: Sees at 6 m what a normal observer sees at 6 m
Sees at 6 m what a normal observer sees at 12 m
w: 6/6 means the patient sees at 6 m what a normal eye sees at 6 m, which is normal acuity. It is not impairment, nor 6/12, nor an inability to read.
k: 6/6 equals normal (top number is test distance, bottom is normal distance). Equal numbers means normal vision.

q: Which instrument is used to measure central corneal thickness?
w: Central corneal thickness is measured with a pachymeter. A keratometer reads curvature, a lensometer lens power, and a radiuscope contact lens curves.
k: Corneal thickness equals pachymeter. 'Pachy' (thick) points to the thickness gauge.

q: Which instrument is commonly used to measure pupil size?
w: Pupil size is measured with a pupillometer, or a simple pupil gauge. A keratometer, radiuscope, and lensometer measure other parameters.
k: Pupil size equals pupillometer. The instrument name carries 'pupil'.

q: Presbyopia is primarily associated with:
o: Loss of accommodative ability with age
w: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation as the lens stiffens, so near focus fails around the forties. It is not axial length, corneal steepening, or detachment.
k: Presbyopia equals aging loss of accommodation. 'Presby' means old; the near-focus fades with age.

q: Which instrument measures the optical power of an ophthalmic lens?
w: A lensometer (focimeter) measures the power of a spectacle or contact lens. A keratometer reads corneal curves, a retinoscope refraction, and a tonometer pressure.
k: Lens power equals lensometer. The instrument that reads a finished lens is the lensometer.

q: A retinoscope is used primarily to:
w: Retinoscopy objectively estimates refractive error by watching the reflex move as you sweep light across the pupil. It is not for pressure, thickness, or direct nerve viewing.
k: Retinoscopy equals objective refraction. Watching the reflex gives the prescription without patient responses.

q: Which test evaluates tear production, using a paper strip?
w: The Schirmer test measures tear production using a paper strip hooked over the lower lid. Snellen, Ishihara, and cover tests measure vision, color, or alignment.
k: Tear production plus paper strip equals Schirmer. The strip that wicks tears is Schirmer.

q: The Schirmer test uses:
w: The Schirmer test uses filter paper strips that absorb tears. It does not use dye alone, prisms, or contact lenses.
k: Schirmer equals filter paper strips. The tool is absorbent paper, not a lens or dye.

q: Under cobalt-blue illumination, fluorescein appears:
w: Under cobalt-blue light, fluorescein fluoresces a bright yellow-green, marking staining and tear film. It does not look black, red, or blue.
k: Fluorescein under blue light glows yellow-green. The excitation is blue, the emission green.

q: Which instrument provides magnified examination of the anterior segment?
w: Magnified examination of the anterior segment is done with the slit lamp biomicroscope. A lensometer, retinoscope, or trial frame do not magnify the eye.
k: Magnified anterior-segment exam equals slit lamp. The go-to front-of-eye microscope.

q: Hyperopia is commonly corrected with:
w: Hyperopia focuses light behind the retina, so a converging plus spherical lens brings it forward. Minus, minus cylinder alone, and prism do not correct it.
k: Plus lens equals hyperopia. The eye that focuses too late needs added converging power.

q: Astigmatism is commonly corrected using:
w: Astigmatism has different power in different meridians, so a cylindrical or toric lens corrects it meridian by meridian. A sphere, prism, or plano lens cannot.
k: Astigmatism equals cylinder/toric correction. Unequal meridians need a cylindrical, not spherical, fix.

q: A significant improvement with pinhole generally suggests:
o: Total irreversible blindness in that eye
Complete destruction of the neural retina
Refractive or optical cause of reduced acuity
Advanced optic nerve atrophy and pallor
w: If a pinhole sharply improves vision, the cause is refractive or optical, since the pinhole removes blur circles. It would not help total blindness, optic atrophy, or a destroyed retina.
k: Pinhole improves equals optical/refractive cause. Disease that destroys the retina or nerve does not respond to a pinhole.

q: Which test evaluates the patient's ability to see colors?
w: The Ishihara test checks the ability to see colors, screening red-green deficiency. Snellen tests acuity, cover tests alignment, Schirmer tears.
k: See colors equals Ishihara. Color plates test color vision.

q: The confrontation test is used to evaluate:
w: The confrontation test screens the visual fields by comparing the patient's to the examiner's. It is not a curvature, accommodation, or pressure test.
k: Confrontation equals field screen. Same as before: face-to-face field check.

q: The near point of accommodation is the closest point at which an object can be seen:
w: The near point of accommodation is the closest distance an object can still be seen clearly, the limit of focusing. Peripheral, without light, or one-eyed conditions are not what it defines.
k: Near point of accommodation equals closest clear point. Clarity is the criterion, not periphery or light.

q: Amplitude of accommodation refers to the:
w: Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum focusing power the eye can add, measured in diopters. It is not pupil size, convergence, or field width.
k: Amplitude of accommodation equals maximum focusing ability. It is the full range of focusing power.

q: The push-up method is commonly used to measure:
w: The push-up method brings a target closer until it blurs to measure amplitude of accommodation. It does not measure pressure, curvature, or color.
k: Push-up equals amplitude of accommodation. Moving a target in until blur gives the amplitude.

q: The accommodative facility test measures the ability to:
w: Accommodative facility measures how quickly the eye can switch focus, usually with plus/minus flippers. It is not a color, field, or thickness test.
k: Facility equals speed of focusing change. 'Facility' points to how fast, not how much.

q: Flipper lenses are commonly used to assess:
w: Flipper (plus/minus) lenses test accommodative facility by forcing rapid focus changes. They do not test field, pressure, or corneal diameter.
k: Flippers equal accommodative facility. The alternating lenses time focusing speed.

q: A narrow slit beam on the slit lamp is particularly useful for examining:
o: Distance visual acuity on a letter chart
w: A narrow slit beam gives a thin optical section, letting the examiner see the layers of transparent structures like the cornea. It is not for blood pressure, acuity, or retinal circulation.
k: Narrow beam equals optical section. A thin slice reveals the depth layers of clear tissue.

q: Which slit lamp technique is useful for examining corneal layers optically?
w: The optical section technique uses a thin slit to view corneal layers in cross-section. Retroillumination, diffuse light, and sclerotic scatter serve other purposes.
k: Corneal layers optically equals optical section. The thin cross-section shows depth.

q: Retroillumination on the slit lamp is useful for detecting:
o: Pupil diameter under dim illumination only
Lens or corneal opacities against a bright background
The vertical height of the palpebral fissure
Small changes in the patient's refractive error
w: Retroillumination bounces light off deeper structures to backlight lens or corneal opacities against a bright background. It does not measure refraction, pupil size, or lid height.
k: Retroillumination equals backlit opacities. Light reflected back from behind reveals opacities.

q: Sclerotic scatter on the slit lamp is useful in detecting:
w: Sclerotic scatter shoots light into the limbus so it travels through the cornea, glowing at any corneal abnormality. It is not for retina, refraction, or optic nerve.
k: Sclerotic scatter equals corneal abnormality detection. Light piped through the cornea lights up defects.

q: Fluorescein examination on the slit lamp can help evaluate:
o: Back vertex power of the lens
w: Fluorescein on the slit lamp evaluates corneal staining and the tear film. It does not read lens power, retinal thickness, or axial length.
k: Fluorescein plus slit lamp equals staining and tear film. Same dye role, viewed magnified.

q: The cover-uncover test is primarily used to detect:
w: The cover-uncover test detects a tropia, a manifest deviation, by watching the covered eye move as it is uncovered. It is not for cataract, ulcer, or color.
k: Cover-uncover equals detect tropia (manifest turn). Watching the just-covered eye reveals a tropia.

q: The alternate cover test is primarily used to measure:
w: The alternate cover test dissociates the eyes and measures the total deviation, both tropia and phoria. It is not an acuity, corneal power, or pupil test.
k: Alternate cover equals total deviation. Rapid alternating cover brings out the full misalignment.

q: The Hirschberg test evaluates:
w: The Hirschberg test judges ocular alignment by where the corneal light reflex falls in each eye. It is not color, tear, or field.
k: Hirschberg equals alignment by corneal reflex. Light reflections show if the eyes point together.

q: Stereopsis refers to:
w: Stereopsis is depth perception built from the two eyes' disparate views. It is not color, central acuity, or peripheral vision.
k: Stereopsis equals depth perception. The 3D sense from two eyes.

q: A receded near point of convergence may indicate difficulty with:
w: A receded (farther) near point of convergence signals convergence difficulty, as the eyes cannot hold single vision up close. It is unrelated to color or distance-only vision.
k: Receded NPC equals convergence problem. A pushed-back near point means weak convergence.

q: The cover test is used primarily to assess:
w: The cover test assesses ocular alignment, revealing phorias and tropias. It is not for color, thickness, or pressure.
k: Cover test equals alignment. Occluding and watching for movement checks how the eyes line up.

q: The alternate cover test is useful for measuring:
w: The alternate cover test measures the total deviation or phoria by fully dissociating the eyes. It is not for acuity, color, or accommodation.
k: Alternate cover equals total deviation/phoria. It uncovers the whole latent-plus-manifest angle.

q: The Maddox rod test is commonly used to evaluate:
w: The Maddox rod turns a light into a line seen by one eye only, revealing a phoria by where the line falls. It is not for acuity, curvature, or color.
k: Maddox rod equals phoria. Dissociating the eyes with a red line measures the latent deviation.

q: The Maddox rod converts a point light source into a:
w: The Maddox rod's cylinders convert a point of light into a streak or line. Not a circle, triangle, or square.
k: Maddox rod equals point into a line. The ridged lens stretches a dot into a streak.

q: The Amsler grid is primarily used to assess the:
w: The Amsler grid assesses the macula, where distortion or gaps signal macular disease. It is not primarily an optic nerve, cornea, or iris test.
k: Amsler grid equals macula. Central grid checks central retina.

q: A patient viewing an Amsler grid may report:
w: A patient with macular disease may see the Amsler grid lines as wavy, called metamorphopsia. Improved color, higher pressure, or better focusing are not grid findings.
k: Amsler complaint equals metamorphopsia (wavy lines). Distortion on the grid signals macular trouble.

q: Contrast sensitivity testing evaluates the ability to:
w: Contrast sensitivity measures the faintest luminance differences a patient can detect, a fuller picture of vision than acuity. It is not color, pressure, or pupil size.
k: Contrast sensitivity equals detecting luminance differences. It grades faint light-dark contrast, not letters alone.

q: Contrast sensitivity may be reduced even when:
w: Contrast sensitivity can be reduced even when Snellen acuity is normal, as in early cataract or optic neuropathy. The other options describe impossible eyes.
k: Contrast loss can hide behind normal acuity. Pick the realistic 'acuity still normal' option.

q: Amsler grid testing is particularly useful for detecting abnormalities involving the:
w: The Amsler grid targets the macula and central vision, catching central distortions. Lids, tear glands, and muscles are not what it tests.
k: Amsler grid equals macula and central vision. Central-field tool, again.

q: A Burton lamp is particularly useful for:
w: A Burton lamp is an ultraviolet-blue lamp with magnifier used to view fluorescein staining and rigid lens fits. It does not measure pressure, axial length, or lens power.
k: Burton lamp equals view fluorescein. UV-blue light plus magnifier shows the dye.

q: The forehead rest on a slit lamp provides:
w: The forehead rest steadies the patient's head against the slit lamp for a stable view. It does not illuminate, magnify, or measure pressure.
k: Forehead rest equals head stabilization. It holds the head still, nothing optical.

q: The joystick of a slit lamp is primarily used to:
w: The joystick moves and focuses the whole slit lamp on the eye. It does not change refraction, read lens power, or alter the cornea.
k: Joystick equals position the instrument. It aims the slit lamp; it changes nothing in the eye.

q: Which filter is commonly used to observe fluorescein on the slit lamp?
w: Fluorescein is best seen through a cobalt-blue filter on the slit lamp. Red, neutral-density, and infrared filters do not excite it.
k: Fluorescein equals cobalt-blue filter. Blue light makes the dye glow.

q: The slit beam on a slit lamp can be adjusted in terms of:
w: The slit beam can be varied in height and width to shape the illumination. Weight, temperature, and color-only are not adjustable beam parameters here.
k: Slit beam adjusts in size (height and width). Think geometry of the beam, not weight or heat.

q: A broad beam of illumination on the slit lamp is useful for:
o: Precise measurement of ocular axial length
Measurement of spectacle lens back power
General examination of the anterior segment
Isolated assessment of pupil light reaction
w: A broad beam floods the anterior segment for a general overview. It does not measure axial length, spectacle power, or pupil reaction.
k: Broad beam equals general anterior-segment survey. Wide light gives the overview.

q: An abnormal or absent red reflex may suggest:
w: An abnormal or absent red reflex suggests a media opacity like cataract blocking the light path. Normal accommodation, color, or alignment would not dull the reflex.
k: Absent red reflex equals media opacity. Something in the light path is blocking it.

q: Pupillary distance can be measured using a:
w: Pupillary distance is measured with a pupillometer (or PD ruler). A tonometer, keratometer, and retinoscope measure other things.
k: PD equals pupillometer. The instrument for the distance between pupils carries the name.

q: The near visual acuity test is commonly performed using:
w: Near acuity is tested with a near vision (reading) chart held at reading distance. Amsler, Ishihara, and Maddox rod test other functions.
k: Near acuity equals near vision chart. A reading card at 40 cm tests near sight.

q: A patient who cannot read the largest letter on a distance chart should be tested using:
o: Ishihara pseudoisochromatic color plates at the near point only
Counting fingers, hand motion, or light perception as appropriate
A red-green duochrome balancing test at six meters only
Central and peripheral corneal keratometry readings only
w: If a patient cannot read the biggest chart letter, you step down to counting fingers, hand motion, then light perception. Ishihara, duochrome, and keratometry are not acuity fallbacks.
k: Below chart letters, drop to CF, HM, LP. Grade the low-vision ladder, not a color or curvature test.

q: Which of the following is important when taking a case history?
o: The chief complaint, symptom duration, and prior ocular history
Only the intraocular pressure measured at this visit
Only the examiner's provisional working diagnosis and plan
Only the objective autorefractor refraction printout
w: A useful case history gathers the chief complaint, how long symptoms have lasted, and previous ocular history together. The examiner's diagnosis, the pressure, and the refraction are findings recorded later, not the history itself.
k: History equals complaint plus duration plus past ocular history combined. Pick the option that lists the patient-reported elements, not a single measured finding.

q: Which instrument is used to assess the corneal surface and anterior chamber under magnification?
w: The corneal surface and anterior chamber are examined under magnification with the slit lamp biomicroscope. A lensometer, radiuscope, or pupillometer do not.
k: Magnified anterior-segment exam equals slit lamp. Same instrument, phrased differently.

q: The primary purpose of a slit lamp biomicroscope is to:
o: Objectively measure the eye's refractive error
Measure the overall axial length of the eye
Record the patient's systemic blood pressure
w: The primary purpose of the slit lamp biomicroscope is to examine ocular structures under magnification. It does not measure refraction, blood pressure, or axial length.
k: Slit lamp equals magnified ocular exam. Its core purpose is looking, magnified.

q: The slit lamp uses a combination of:
w: The slit lamp works by combining magnification with a focused slit of illumination. Not ultrasound, X-rays, or tonometry and retinoscopy.
k: Slit lamp equals magnification plus focused light. The two-part name gives the two parts.

q: Which component of the slit lamp produces the slit beam of light?
w: The illumination system of the slit lamp produces the adjustable slit beam. The microscope, chin rest, and joystick do other jobs.
k: Slit beam comes from the illumination system. The light source makes the light.

q: The microscope of a slit lamp provides:
w: The microscope part of the slit lamp gives magnified viewing of the eye. It does not illuminate, measure pressure, or read curvature.
k: Microscope equals magnified viewing. The viewing half magnifies; the lamp half lights.

q: The chin rest of a slit lamp is used to:
w: The chin rest stabilizes the patient's head for a steady slit lamp exam. It does not measure thickness, adjust light, or test acuity.
k: Chin rest equals head stabilization. It holds the patient still.

q: The primary purpose of preliminary testing in optometry is to:
o: Perform minor ocular surgery before any other diagnostic testing is done
Immediately prescribe and dispense contact lenses to the patient
Measure only the intraocular pressure during the first visit encounter
Establish baseline information about the patient's visual and ocular status
w: Preliminary testing exists to establish baseline information about the patient's visual and ocular status before deeper testing. It is not for immediate lenses, surgery, or pressure alone.
k: Prelim testing equals gather baseline data. The purpose is a starting picture, not treatment.

q: Which test is commonly performed first to assess visual acuity?
w: Visual acuity is usually assessed first with the Snellen test. Schirmer (tears), Amsler (macula), and Maddox rod (phoria) test other functions.
k: First acuity check equals Snellen. The letter chart leads the exam.

q: Visual acuity is commonly recorded as:
w: Visual acuity is recorded as a fraction like 6/6 or 20/20. It is not in mmHg, diopters, or prism diopters.
k: Acuity equals 6/6 or 20/20 notation. The Snellen fraction is the unit.

q: Which test measures unaided visual acuity?
w: Unaided visual acuity is measured with the unaided (no correction) acuity test. Keratometry, tonometry, and pachymetry measure other parameters.
k: Unaided acuity equals the unaided acuity test. 'Without glasses' still just means an acuity chart.

q: The pinhole test is useful for determining whether reduced visual acuity may be improved by:
w: The pinhole shows whether blurred acuity would improve by correcting refractive error, since it removes optical blur. It does not work by raising light, pressure, or changing pupil color.
k: Pinhole equals would refraction help. It isolates the refractive component of blur.

q: Retinoscopy is primarily used to determine:
w: Retinoscopy objectively determines refractive error by neutralizing the pupil reflex. It is not for tears, pressure, or color.
k: Retinoscopy equals objective refractive error. The reflex neutralization gives the prescription.

q: During retinoscopy, the examiner observes the:
w: During retinoscopy the examiner watches the retinal reflex move in the pupil to judge the error. Corneal thickness, pupil diameter, and tear meniscus are not observed.
k: Retinoscopy watches the retinal reflex. The moving red glow in the pupil is what you neutralize.

q: The red reflex can be evaluated using a:
w: The red reflex is checked with a direct ophthalmoscope held at arm's length. A keratometer, lensometer, and pupillometer do not show it.
k: Red reflex equals direct ophthalmoscope. The handheld scope reveals the reflex.

q: What instrument is used to measure the horizontal visible iris diameter (HVID)?
w: The horizontal visible iris diameter is measured with a corneal measuring gauge (a millimeter reticule). A keratometer, lensometer, and tonometer measure other things.
k: HVID equals corneal measuring gauge. A linear diameter needs a millimeter scale.

q: The Hirschberg test is primarily used to assess:
w: The Hirschberg test assesses ocular alignment from the position of the corneal light reflex. It is not a color, acuity, or contrast test.
k: Hirschberg equals alignment. Corneal reflex position tells if the eyes are straight.

q: The red reflex test can help identify:
w: An abnormal red reflex helps identify a media opacity such as cataract. Phoria, color deficiency, and accommodation problems do not change the reflex.
k: Red reflex test equals detect media opacity. A blocked reflex means something clouding the media.

q: A slit lamp with a fluorescein evaluation is useful for assessing:
o: Systemic blood pressure and pulse rate
Overall spectacle frame and temple size
w: A slit lamp with fluorescein assesses how a lens centers and where the cornea stains. It does not judge frame size, blood pressure, or color.
k: Slit lamp plus fluorescein equals lens fit and corneal staining. The dye shows centration and surface breaks.

q: Which instrument can be used to assess tear film stability?
w: Tear film stability is assessed on the slit lamp by watching the fluorescein film break up. A lensometer, radiuscope, and retinoscope cannot.
k: Tear film stability equals slit lamp (with fluorescein). The film breakup is watched under magnification.

q: Tear breakup time is commonly evaluated using:
w: Tear breakup time is measured with fluorescein viewed on the slit lamp, timing the first dry spot. A lensometer, keratometer alone, or trial frame will not.
k: TBUT equals fluorescein plus slit lamp. Dye plus timing gives film stability.

q: The Worth 4 Dot test evaluates:
w: The Worth 4 Dot evaluates binocular sensory status, showing fusion or suppression. It is not for thickness, pressure, or acuity alone.
k: Worth 4 Dot equals binocular sensory status. Fusion versus suppression, again.

q: The duochrome test commonly uses:
w: The duochrome test presents red and green fields to balance the spherical endpoint. Blue/yellow, black/white, and orange/violet are not used.
k: Duochrome equals red and green fields. The two-color balance test.

q: The Amsler grid is primarily used to evaluate:
w: The Amsler grid evaluates macular function, flagging central distortion or scotoma. It is not for pressure, curvature, or alignment.
k: Amsler grid equals macular function. Central-vision map.

q: Distortion of straight lines on the Amsler grid is called:
w: Wavy or bent straight lines on the Amsler grid are metamorphopsia, a macular sign. Diplopia, photophobia, and scotoma describe other problems.
k: Distorted grid lines equal metamorphopsia. 'Morph' means distorted shape.

q: Visual acuity is the ability to:
w: Visual acuity is the ability to resolve fine spatial detail, such as separating tiny letters. It is not brightness detection, pressure, or accommodation.
k: Acuity equals resolving fine detail. Sharpness of detail, not brightness or focusing.

q: Which instrument is best for detailed examination of the cornea and anterior segment?
w: The slit lamp is best for detailed examination of the cornea and anterior segment. A keratometer, lensometer, or pupillometer serve narrower roles.
k: Detailed cornea and anterior segment equals slit lamp. The front-of-eye microscope wins.
